implementation_notes: Go has no classes and no static members, so the singleton is a package-level variable plus an accessor function, with sync.Once performing the one-time initialisation; the package itself is the namespace that replaces the private constructor and the well-known access point. Since Go 1.21 sync.OnceValue (with OnceFunc/OnceValues) wraps the same guarantee into a function value and removes the separate once/result variables. Keep the Once next to the value it guards and never copy it, and return a pointer so callers cannot reassign the package variable.
pitfalls: Copying a struct that embeds sync.Once (or passing it by value) breaks the guarantee: keep it in a package-level variable or behind a pointer.

Package-level variables and init() functions run before main in a compiler-determined order across files, so a singleton built there can observe another package's state that is not ready; prefer lazy accessors.
sync.Once.Do treats a panicking action as done (later calls do not retry), while sync.OnceValue re-panics with the same value on every call: the two error semantics must be chosen deliberately.
Package state lives as long as the test binary: tests share the instance unless it is injected, and t.Parallel() tests must not mutate it.

variants.name: sync.OnceValue closure
variants.implementation_notes: Since Go 1.21 the initialisation can be expressed as a function value: var Get = sync.OnceValue(load) performs the load once and returns the cached result on every call, hiding the state inside the closure instead of three package-level names. It is the tidier default for a single computed value and unsuitable when the initialiser needs runtime arguments or must retry after a failure (a panicking loader panics on every call) - fall back to sync.Once or a singleflight-backed loader there.
pitfalls: Get becomes a variable rather than a function: taking its address or wrapping it in an interface changes shape, and a test can replace the whole function value.
OnceValue requires a no-argument loader, so runtime parameters must be captured in a closure at construction time.
A panicking loader re-panics identically on every call - there is no retry path.
